name: Sivakozhundeeswarar Temple, Theerthanagiri (Thiruthinainagar)
deity: Shiva as Sivakozhundeeswarar, with the goddess Oppila Nayaki
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu between Cuddalore and Chidambaram, sung by Sundarar in the Tevaram (8th century)
dynasty: Village temple of the Tevaram age, renewed over the centuries
summary: At Theerthanagiri, the Thiruthinainagar of the Tevaram, Shiva is worshipped as Sivakozhundeeswarar, remembered as the aged guest who ate a farmer's millet and then worked his field.

sections.history: Theerthanagiri is a village of Cuddalore district lying roughly midway between Cuddalore and Chidambaram, and its Shiva temple is the Thiruthinainagar of the Tevaram. It is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and is counted among the shrines of Nadu Nadu, the middle country between the Chola and Pallava lands. Sundarar sang the Lord of Thinainagar in his hymns; the Lord's name, Sivakozhundu, means the tender shoot of Shiva. The old name, the town of thinai or foxtail millet, preserves the farming story at the heart of the shrine, and the temple remains a village temple, cared for by the people of the surrounding fields.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east and is entered through a three-tiered rajagopuram, beyond which a walled enclosure holds the sanctum of the lingam and the separate shrine of the goddess Oppila Nayaki, she who has no equal. The sacred tree is the kondrai, the Indian laburnum with its hanging golden blossoms, and the temple tank is the Jambava theertham, named for Jambavan, the wise bear-king of the Ramayana, whom tradition remembers as a worshipper here.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells of a farmer named Periyan and his wife, devotees of Shiva who would not eat until they had fed at least one fellow devotee each day. One day the Lord himself came to them as an old man. They had only millet to give, and he ate it gladly; then, in return for the meal, he helped them cultivate their land. The couple's humble hospitality is remembered in the village's name, and the Lord here is honoured as one who repays the simplest offering.
sections.festivals: The great festival is the thirteen-day brahmotsavam in Vaikasi (May–June). Maha Shivaratri in Masi, the Annabhishekam in Aippasi, when the lingam is covered in cooked rice, and Arudra Darshanam in Margazhi are also observed, with the monthly Pradosham. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Theerthanagiri is a peaceful farming village, and its story suits it: the Lord who sat down to a meal of millet and then took up the plough. Worship at the sanctum, visit Oppila Nayaki in her shrine, and pause by the Jambava theertham and the kondrai tree. The temple is an easy stop on the road between Cuddalore and Chidambaram.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples of the region. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Theerthanagiri lies about 25 km from Chidambaram and about 27 km from Cuddalore, near Alapakkam; buses between Cuddalore and Chidambaram serve the area. Cuddalore and Chidambaram are the convenient railway stations, and Puducherry is the nearest airport, with Chennai the nearest major international airport.
